contributions.headingText: Neuroendocrine carcinoma (NEC) is an invasive carcinoma characterized by high-grade neuroendocrine morphology (small cell or large cell), supported by the presence of neurosecretory granules and a diffuse, uniform immunoreactivity for neuroendocrine markers.

8246/3 Neuroendocrine carcinoma NOS

8041/3 Neuroendocrine carcinoma, small cell

8013/3 Neuroendocrine carcinoma, large cell

2C6Y & XH0U20 Other specified malignant neoplasms of breast & Neuroendocrine carcinoma NOS

2C6Y & XH9SY0 Other specified malignant neoplasms of breast & Small cell neuroendocrine carcinoma

2C6Y & XH0NL5 Other specified malignant neoplasms of breast & Large cell neuroendocrine carcinoma

Acceptable: small cell carcinoma; large cell neuroendocrine carcinoma.

Not recommended: poorly differentiated neuroendocrine carcinoma.
Small cell neuroendocrine carcinoma; large cell neuroendocrine carcinoma

There are no notable or specific differences in presentation from other high-grade breast carcinomas. Clinical syndromes related to hormone production are not documented. Patient age ranges from 43 to 70 years {15976350; 10976697}. Tumour size ranges from 1.3 to 5.0 cm (mean: 2.6 cm) {10976697}. Approximately 40% of small cell carcinomas have nodal metastasis {25853028}. In three population-based studies of patients with primary small cell NECs (SCNECs) of the breast {25853028; 19563623; 25885914}, 70–81% had localized disease (local or regional) and 19–30% had distant metastasis. Lymph node positivity was reported in 41% of the cases {25853028}.

Primary NECs of the breast are extremely rare. SCNECs account for approximately 0.1% of all breast cancers {25853028} and for 3–10% of extrapulmonary small cell carcinomas {19563623; 25885914; 21618245}. Large cell NECs (LCNECs) are extremely rare.
There are no data on the etiology of NECs, but they probably have the same etiology as other high-grade breast carcinomas. No link with cigarette smoking has been reported.

Of the 9 SCNECs of the breast reported by Shin et al. {10976697}, 3 cases were associated with invasive, poorly differentiated duct carcinoma, and ductal carcinoma in situ was seen in 7 tumours – 5 were of the small cell type in ducts and 2 were of the ductal type with high nuclear grade. These findings suggest that SCNECs result from a specific line of differentiation of mammary cancer stem cells towards neuroendocrine / small cell–type differentiation, which can take place at the in situ stage or later (at the invasive stage), rather than resulting from the malignant transformation of specific neuroendocrine cells in the normal breast tissue. In a way akin to lung SCNECs, breast SCNECs display TP53 and RB1 somatic genetic alterations in as many as 75% and 19% of cases, respectively {27329168}. Data on the pathogenesis of LCNEC are lacking.

Primary NECs have no gross features distinct from those of other types of high-grade breast cancer. They can present with poorly circumscribed, fleshy, white to tan cut surfaces and focal areas of necrosis.

Histologically and immunohistochemically, NECs are morphologically indistinguishable from their counterparts in the lung {29661717; 26960398}. SCNECs display an infiltrative growth pattern and are composed of densely packed, fairly uniform, small, dark hyperchromatic cells that have a high N:C ratio, scant cytoplasm, inconspicuous nucleoli, and poorly defined cytoplasmic borders. In LCNEC, the cells show evident cytoplasm and highly pleomorphic nuclei with variably coarse chromatin. Common features of both SCNEC and LCNEC are high numbers of mitotic figures and focal areas of necrosis. An in situ component with the same cytological features may be detected. Lymphatic tumour emboli are frequently encountered {15976350; 10976697}.

The differential diagnoses of primary SCNEC include metastatic small cell carcinoma of non-mammary origin (most commonly from the lung), Merkel cell carcinoma, lymphoma, and melanoma. The presence of an associated ductal carcinoma in situ or conventional-type mammary carcinoma component confirms the primary nature of the tumour. SCNEC should also be differentiated from some forms of the high-grade solid subtype of adenoid cystic carcinoma, metaplastic carcinomas or ductal of no special type (NST) with basaloid cells and an increased N:C ratio. LCNEC should be differentiated from high-grade invasive breast carcinoma NST, by the presence of extensive neuroendocrine differentiation, and from metastatic LCNEC of non-mammary origin (i.e. from the lung).

FNA of SCNEC shows the presence of malignant cells with small cell phenotypes, which may display nuclear moulding, finely granular or salt-and-pepper chromatin, and scant delicate cytoplasm. Necrosis is frequently present in cytological samples of NEC.

Immunohistochemical analysis shows consistent staining for cytokeratin markers but variable staining for neuroendocrine markers, with more than two thirds of cases staining positively for chromogranin and synaptophysin. PGP9.5, CD56 (NCAM), and NSE are positive in the majority of cases. SCNECs are positive for BCL2 and negative for ERBB2 (HER2) {10976697}. ER positivity has been reported in 30–50% of cases {10976697; 27329168} and PR positivity in a smaller proportion, but other authors did not identify receptor expression in SCNEC {18357385}. TTF1 expression in SCNEC of the breast has been reported, but not diffuse strong nuclear staining as seen in small cell carcinoma of the lung {20661411; 19578049}. GATA3 expression has been reported in NEC of the breast but not in metastatic NECs, including those from the lung {27125358}.

Essential: histological features similar to those of SCNEC and LCNEC of the lung; high-grade tumour.

Desirable: coexisting ductal carcinoma in situ.
NECs are staged similarly to other types of invasive breast carcinoma.

SCNEC is significantly associated with a worse prognosis than other neuroendocrine tumours (NETs) of the breast {25399232}. The outcomes of patients with breast SCNEC were superior to those of patients with stage-matched small cell lung carcinoma, except in patients with distant disease {25853028}. It was reported that radiation therapy is not associated with a significant difference in survival for patients with either localized or regional disease {25853028}. Localized SCNEC is usually managed similarly to usual ductal breast cancer. In the metastatic SCNEC setting, regimens that are implemented in small cell lung cancer are usually attempted. There is some evidence that ER-positive SCNEC may respond to hormone therapy {22424945}. LCNECs of the breast are rare, and no clinical data on prognosis are available.
